He wakes up lazily, and with his eyes still glued shut, he manages to find his owners' scent as they walk through the door. He is so tiny (barely a baby) that he still can’t coordinate his movements very well. He trips over his own paws, just learning to walk. With his head down, eyes on the floor, and uncoordinated steps, he always finds his way to his owners' feet. He has learned to rub against them, greet them, and show his happiness.

He tries to meow to say welcome, but he’s so freshly awakened that he can’t manage more than a raspy “mew,” one of those early morning sounds with vocal cords that haven’t warmed up yet.

Little by little, he wakes up, his voice clears, and he starts meowing loudly, almost shouting. He loves being picked up, and once off the ground, he begins to explain all the things he did today. He does this with his eyes, his meows, and by placing his paws on their faces, touching as if trying to emphasize the importance of his tale. It’s like someone persistently tapping another’s shoulder to get their attention.

If they don’t engage in the conversation, he gets upset; he wants real attention, not just preaching to the wind. So, his owners spend some time talking with him in their arms, sharing the delights of the day that’s ending.

He feels excited and happy when he talks to his owners, his joy tinged with a bit of anxiety. This anxiety leads him straight to his food bowl, where he dives in headfirst to crunch his kibble. The hard, crunchy “creck-creck” of his teeth echoes off the kitchen tiles. It’s always nice to hear that sound, the murmur of health, and it's good to breathe a little health into the house.

Next, he puts on a pitiful face to see if he can get something from the fridge. He’s very good at it. He loves sweet ham and has quickly learned to associate the fridge with his favorite treat. He approaches the fridge, leans on it with his front paws, looks at his owners, and meows loudly. If that doesn’t work (and it usually doesn’t), he sits at their feet, looking up in such a perpendicular way that it’s scary; it seems like he might break his neck. He’s so small that from above, all you can see is his head and eyes. Those eyes with that pitiful look can melt any heart, no matter how cold.

Usually, the owners resist the temptation, and he doesn’t get his treat, so he heads back to his food bowl to crunch a few more pieces of kibble that all taste the same. Nothing like the delicious sweet ham.

After eating, he wants to play, of course. Regardless of the tasks his owners have to do. At this point, he dances around their feet, trying (and succeeding) to bite their shoelaces, hugging their legs, and clinging with his claws... In general, demanding attention that he was denied during the day while he napped alone at home.

The house is big for such a small cat, and his companion is a fat, lazy Russian hamster who ignores his presence. But it’s just a façade; the hamster knows perfectly well who’s lurking down there. Though he pretends to be tough and sleeps as if he isn’t scared, everyone is aware that he’s slightly terrified since this strange, bigger, and hairier animal intruded into his life.

Still, he hides it well, and the kitten, despite trying, doesn’t find a playmate in him. Besides, the hamster is quite old and isn’t up for much partying; he prefers to close his eyes and pretend it’s not happening.

So, the kitten plays alone with his toys, cushions, stray socks on the rug, even his own tail... He stays entertained all day, no denying that. But when his owners come home, well, that’s another story.

Now it’s playtime because he’s earned it and has the right to it, so those big humans better pay attention because that’s why they have him at home.

With more or less enthusiasm, his owners start to reciprocate: they pick him up, toss him on the floor, let him bite and scratch, scratch his belly, hide toys, and play with him. It’s his favorite time of the day, playing with his owners. He tries not to go overboard and not bite or scratch too hard, but sometimes he gets carried away and lands a couple of well-aimed swipes. The owners don’t like that and sometimes grab him by the scruff and lift him off the ground. He doesn’t like that; it reminds him of when his mother scolded him. He reflexively goes still and stares straight ahead. Then, his owners look him in the eyes and scold him. He doesn’t quite understand what they’re saying, but he recognizes the tone and the situation. Okay... maybe he got a little too excited, he won’t do it again, but please put him down. After a while, he forgets and has to take flight again for a few moments. What can you expect from a baby kitten?

Soon, he’s exhausted and falls asleep on the sofa between his two owners, where it’s warm, or on one of their laps. He curls up and surrenders to sleep. He still doesn’t quite understand his own body and biorhythms; his heart is small and beats quickly and strongly. When he wakes up, he has that look of not knowing where he is or what just happened.

He loves getting into bed with his owners. Not necessarily to sleep because he loves to play the most, and he bites their feet, pajamas, and the blanket. He jumps, trying to catch hands under the sheets. He hides, stalks, wiggles his butt, and jumps as if his life depends on it. He needs to improve his technique, though. He jumps with all four paws spread, all claws out, and mouth wide open. Not that he’ll encounter any natural enemies in his home, but that “all-out” technique never yielded good results in nature.

Sooner or later, he tires out again and falls asleep at the foot of the bed. The owners take him to the living room and place him in his bed. He has a wonderful soft blue bed. A toy monkey sleeps with him, one that, judging by its shirt, has traveled all the way to the United States. Still, he doesn’t like his bed too much; he prefers the warmth of his owners, who let him in from time to time. He thinks it won’t last long and that when he’s a bit older, they’ll make him sleep in his bed, but while he can, he wants to take advantage. He loves their smell and warmth.

In the morning, he gets a bit bored when the sun comes up and walks across his still-sleeping owners’ faces, purring loudly, indignant at their indifference.

Finally, he gets the attention he seeks, and they get up. Good: now he can run under their feet, jump, and play as he likes.

Just before collapsing in exhaustion again, of course.
